speakeroldname: Hon. R. J. MANION (Minister of Railways and Canals):
subtopic: REDUCTION OP DOMESTIC RATES ON GRAIN AND GRAIN PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday I
promised to make to the house a very brief statement concerning domestic freight rates, and particularly concerning the relation of that matter to the bill standing in the name of the 'hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid), and the resolution in the name of the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Perley). At various times other hon. members from the western provinces have asked questions concerning this matter. May I point out that during the interprovincial conference a meeting was held at which were traffic representatives of the two railway systems, and two representatives from each of the four western provinces, with the exception of British Columbia. On account of Doctor Tolmie's loss there was only one representative from that province. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir), and myself, attended the meeting, and there was an endeavour to arrive at some satisfactory solution of the difficulties, and to formulate at least a compromise among the different parties concerned.
As a result of the conference a satisfactory arrangement was arrived at. Although I do not intend at this time to give details, I may say that after a lengthy discussion, a proposal was made by myself to cut the domestic rate materially on the lower grades of grain- feed grain. The intent was not to get the rate as low as the export rate, but to cut it materially. That suggestion was satisfactory to the representatives of the four western provinces, as expressed by them at that time, and in a general way was acceptable also to the representatives of the railways, who agreed to take the matter under advisement and to submit to me a letter officially offering to put into force the rates proposed on the lower grades of grain, or that type known as feed grain. This would affect particularly the poultry raisers. From the information we have received the greatest number of complaints concerning the freight rate between the prairie provinces and British Columbia had come from the poultry raisers.

speechtext: There is no dispute between the prairie provinces and British Columbia; it is between eastern Canada and British Columbia.

I refer to the dispute between the western provinces and the railways. The railway representatives were to receive from the Department of Agriculture a list of the lower grades of grain which could be used for feed purposes, and some time was required to get this information. Unfortunately one of the representatives, the traffic manager of the Canadian Pacific Railway, Mr. Stephen became ill and as a consequence the proposal has not been placed in my hands, but it is my expectation that within a day or two I shall receive it. At that time I shall send it to the representatives of the provinces. They are to deal with it, and if it is acceptable to them they will advise me and the new rate will be put into effect.
In view of the proposed compromise arrangement I suggest to the hon. members for New Westminster and Qu'Appelle, and to any other hon. members interested that they might well leave the matter in abeyance until we have had the opportunity to get replies from the western provinces.

Mr. ,T. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre) moved:
Whereas under our present economic arrangement large numbers of our people are unemployed and without the means of earning a livelihood for themselves and their dependents;
And whereas the prevalence of the present depression throughout the world indicates fundamental defects in the existing economic system;
Therefore be it resolved,-That, in the opinion of this house, the government should immediately take measures looking to the setting up of a cooperative commonwealth in which all natural resources and the socially necessary machinery of production will be used in the interests of the people and not for the benefit of the few.
He said: All down through the years there have been those who dreamed of a new and better social order. I do not know that it was
ever better expressed than by our own English poet Blake, who would give us no respite until "we have built Jerusalem in England's green and pleasant land." Prophets have foretold the coming of a better day. Great economists have pointed out that our present economic system could not last very long, but must give place to a different one. In more recent days we have the technicians pointing out not only the feasibility of fundamental changes in our social order, but the absolute necessity of such changes if our civilization is to persist.
It is only the newer groups, however, that have had the courage to set this before the country in the form of a definite program. When the Independent Labour party was first represented in this house in 1921, we placed in the very beginning of our platform the following:
The Independent Labour party of Manitoba is formed for the purpose of giving political expression to the aspirations of all workers regardless of industrial affiliation, who believe in the establishment of a cooperative commonwealth, with production for use and not for profit as its economic basis.
As far as opportunity offered I have tried through the years to keep that object definitely in view. Last year the United Farmers of Alberta, in order that there should be no doubt about their ultimate objective, stated their position in very clear terms, adopting the following short definition of a cooperative commonwealth:
A comniunity freed from the domination of irresponsible financial and economic power, in which all social means of production and distribution, including land, are socially owned and controlled either by voluntarily organized groups of producers and consumers, or-in the case of the major public services and utilities and such productive and distributive enterprises as can be conducted most efficiently when owned in common-by public corporations responsible to the people's elected representatives.
When I introduced this motion a year ago there was no large body of organized opinion behind it. Today that situation is altered, for last August there was organized the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation-

a federation of organizations whose purpose is the establishment in Canada of a cooperative commonwealth in which the basic principle regulating production, distribution and exchange will be the supply of human needs instead of the making of profits.
The statement given to the public at that time, and embodied in resolutions by the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, goes on:
The object of the federation shall be to promote cooperation between the member organizations and to correlate their political activities.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The hon. gentleman misunderstood me. It would mean the entire wiping out of the present federal system, if effect were given to what has just been said.

No, Mr. Speaker, that is not correct. I would point out further that this new organization is a federation rather than a party. The farm bodies in the three western provinces and in Ontario have already voted to affiliate. Further than that, the political labour bodies in the provinces from British Columbia to Montreal have also voted to affiliate. And in addition a very large number of people who have been outside the ranks of farmer or labour political parties are now joining Cooperative Commonwealth Federation clubs, and will in this way come into the federation.
May I say that the name is descriptive of the basis and purpose of the new organization. It does not advocate a bureaucratic state socialism. We recognize very clearly that there are certain matters which must be dealt with by the state; there are other matters that may be left to voluntary cooperative effort. We clearly emphasized that in one of the planks of our platform, if I may use that term-the encouragement of all cooperative enterprises which are steps to the attainment of the cooperative commonwealth.
The Prime Minister, who has already voiced his objection thus early in my speech, gave a rather curious reception to the new organization. In his speech in Toronto last NovemfM*\ Woodsworth.!
ber, as reported in the Mail and Empire of November 10, 1932, he said:
The "swing to the left" behind Mr. Woodsworth is towards a government soviet in its character. ... It is no longer a party but a jumble, being led by a cooperative commonwealth. Why? Because they seek to capitalize all the unrest that exists.
Hear, hear.
The Prime Minister or the Conservative party ought never to talk about capitalizing unrest.
In this he is right I

The Prime Minister goes on:
What do they offer you for dumping you in the mud? Socialism, communism, dictatorship.
. . . They are sowing their seeds everywhere. . . . And we know that throughout Canada this propaganda is being put forward by organizations from foreign lands that seek to destroy our institutions. And we ask every man and woman to put the iron heel of ruthlessness against a thing of that kind.
Hear, hear.
There are some hon. gentlemen behind the Prime Minister who applaud.
A lot of them.
I want to say to the Prime Minister that his statement is not only libellous, but it is clearly seditious.

Does that come under
section 98 of the criminal code?

No, it comes under sections which are much more fundamental to the welfare of this country than section 98. It is setting one class against another. It is advocating the use of force, and as such I say that it is clearly seditious, and further it is absolutely untrue. I wonder what would be suggested if I should advocate putting the iron heel of ruthlessness on all capitalists?
On the neck of the Prime Minister.

Or, as has just
been suggested to me, on the neck of the Prime Minister? I am quite sure that certain sections of the criminal code would be immediately invoked. In all seriousness I think it is beneath the dignity of the Prime Minister to make a speech of that kind. The Prime Minister is very fond of quoting scripture. May I venture to recall to his memory a certain passage in which the one whom he calls the Man of Nazareth says "with what measure you mete, it shall be measured to you again."

Cooperative Commonwealth-Mr. Woodsworth
I may say that the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation has no connection what-;ver with Moscow-none whatever.

If some of the
gentlemen who say "oh" would have the courage to get up and make the statement that their interjection implies, they would have to retract. It is all very well for men hiding behind high positions to make baseless allegations against other citizens of this country, but the least they can do, is to prove their allegations, and the Prime Minister has the whole secret service at his disposal to try to prove his. The Cooperative Commonwealth Federation is an indepedent organization, and it is preposterous-
Hear, hear.

-that the labour men of this country from coast to coast, and further, the organized farmers in the four great provinces, should back an organization of that kind only to have it suggested that it emanates from Moscow. The Conservative; say that. On the other hand, the Liberals say that it is a Tory trick. You caD take your choice.
Let me say that we must distinguish clearly between the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation and communism. It is quite true that both believe in a changed social order, in a new economic system. The communists are convinced that this can be brought about only by violence. They think it cannot be done in any other way. We believe that it may come in Canada by peaceful methods and in an orderly fashion, and that is the purpose of this organization.
The end being the same.

It may very well
be that force may prove inevitable, yes, if the attitude of certain gentlemen is persisted in and the people of this country are denied the right that they have to self-expression and to the enjoyment of a decent livelihood.
Mr. GARLAND l Bow River): Even the right to work is denied them.

I note that the
Vancouver Daily Province in its .ssue of December 6, said this:
The answer is that you cannot effect such a revolution at once, if at all, wi*h >ut force and violence. You cannot destroy coupon clipping *without tearing down the intricate and allinvolving structure of capitalism, and you cannot do that without misery and universal suffering and injustice and tyranny.
Well, if many take the position that we cannot do this thing constitutionally, and 53719-107
behind it is the threat that it will not be permitted to be done constitutionally, then none of us can answer as to what may actually take place. We in our group are out to try to bring about the end in view by peaceful and orderly methods.
The Prime Minister goes on to say:
Remember the words of the Man of Nazareth, "the poor we have always with us." Nineteen centuries have passed, but it still is so.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, positively sickening that a wealthy man should stand up and lecture poor people in that fashion. Only a week ago, when I was addressing a iarge meeting of unemployed married men in Calgary, the Prime Minister's own city, I thought how insufferable it was that the Prime Minister should talk to these men in that fashion and offer them that kind of moralizing, when he himself enjoys bis own wealth because of certain social arrangements, and when his policies, in the judgment of a great many people of this country, have done much to bring about the impoverishment of these poor people.
What have you done for this country?

I would appeal to
you, Mr. Speaker, for order. I am, I think, within my rights. Certain gentlemen are constantly interrupting and I would appeal to you that they either leave the chamber or be silenced. As a matter of fact, I do not think the Prime Minister is interpreting scripture in accord with the interpretation of a great many of the most eminent theologians. May I venture to quote a paragraph from a very interesting pamphlet, Catholic Principles and the Present Crisis, issued by the Reverend John A. Ryan, D.D., in which he says:
We cannot perm:, millions to starve in this land of plenty nor can we afford to unleash the forces of savagery and revolution. In the extreme predicament that is closer to us than we like to contemplate, there is another Catholic principle which is pertinent and adequate. It was .-.rated by Pope Leo XIII in an Encyclical On the Condition of Labour: "Whenever the general interest or any particular class suffers or is threatened with injury which in no other way can be met or prevented, it is the duty of the public authority to intervene."
Father Ryan goes on to say:
If for any reason the public works remedy fails, the public authorities will be under moral obligation to take temporary charge of and operate our essential industries, not only for the benefit of our most distressed classes but in the interest of the whole community.
Showing the bankruptcy of capitalism in this crisis, may I quote a paragraph from

Hjalmar Schact, until lately president of the German Reichsbank, who in a recent book said :
Never was the incapacity of the economic leaders of the capitalist world so glaringly demonstrated as today. A capitalism which cannot feed the workers of the world has no right to exist. The guilt of the capitalist system lies in ite alliance with the violent policies of imperialism and militarism. The ruling classes of the world today have as completely failed in political leadership as in economic.
We believe that the first step to be taken in bettering the present conditions is to adopt a planned economy. During the war, when the lit e of the nation was considered to be at stake, there was very careful planning not only within our own country but as between the allied nations, and rationing was carried out to a very considerable extent. Within the nation as a whole, however, we normally have permitted anarchy to reign; we have had overdevelopment in some lines and underdevelopment in others. Take our pulp and paper as an outstanding example of the absence of any definite plan-overcapitalization and overdevelopment of every kind going on until even Saturday Night describes the power project as a racket.
I do not need to dwell on this; it is known to everyone. Moreover, we have had manipulation of credit which has played serious mischief with our whole economic system and has transferred hundreds of millions of dollars from one set of pockets to another. Further than that, we have had no relationship existing between distribution or consumption and producticn It is obvious that our machine must slow down unless the people can buy whac is produced Had I time I could easily give a great many quotations from recognized authorities on this point.
One of the most recent pronouncements was contained in a resolution passed by the international labour organization. Mr. P. W. Martin, summarizing the conference resolution, says:
By means of the special financing of public works, it aims at increasing the volume oi buying-the fundamental condition of any improvement in the economic situation. By insisting upon monetary stability it provides for tile essential measure which must accompany any such increase in the volume of buying, viz., adequate safeguards against undesirable price inflation. By laying down that the achievement of monetary stability must be international ir, scope it makes the necessary basic provision for the achievement of exchange stability Finally by drawing attention to the need foi non-nionetary measures, the adoption of which would be facilitated by the monetary measures already considered, it opens the way to international action for adjusting production to consumption and removing the barriers to inter-
[Mr. Woodsworth.J
national trade. . . . For the irrational forces which at present control business activity it proposes to substitute a process better adapted to modern conditions; conscious adjustment of the volume of buying, so as to provide an adequate outlet for the whole product of industry, no matter how large that product may be. And in making this proposal it goes to the root of the present crisis.
In this connection I may give one other quotation taken from the October letter of the Royal Bank of Canada. Speaking of changes, he says:
Among the most notable has been the attention given in the last few years to national planning-an idea developed in a rapid and spectacular form by the Russians, but of necessity forcing itself upon all of us. . . . We have scarcely grasped the fact that individualism in the old sense is no longer possible and that laissez-faire and the invisible hand are out-dated, when we are compelled to acknowledge that cooperation on a base even so broad as the national one is inadequate. In fact, its consequences are far more serious. Disasters may follow from an unregulated and individualistic economic behaviour, but they are mild compared with the tragedies if large national groups clash, each thoroughly organized in opposition to the rest. The national approach will not do.
I do not think we could proceed very far along the line of central planning-that is, under an administration really in earnest about producing results-without having to deal with the control of the banks. Theoretically, of course, parliament controls the banks, but in practice, in my judgment, the banks control the administration. Back as early as 1925 I introduced a resolution to this effect:
It is not in the interests of the country at large that the privilege of issuing currency and controlling financial credit should be granted to private corporations.
I am more than ever convinced that the issuing of currency and the control of financial credit should be in the hands of a body directly responsible to the representatives of the people. It may be that we can set up i commission, although the commission form of government is today on trial; but it ought aot to be left to those who might rightly be termed irresponsible and interested parties. Whether or not it is necessary to nationalize our whole banking system is perhaps a matter for debate, but all that we insist upon is that there should be effective control, and that may probably be exercised through a central bank working in the interests of the people rather than in the interests of the banks.
I do not think we could proceed very far without increasing the public control of industry. I believe the Prime Minister himself stated the underlying principle that should

obtain in dealing with our natural resources, m his speech introducing the radio bill last year. This is what he said:
I believe that there is no government in i nnada that does not regret today that it has nai ted with some of these natural resources for considerations wholly inadequate and on terms that do not reflect the principle under which the crown holds the natural resources in trust, for all the people. . . .
If the Prime Minister would extend that principle to all our natural resources he would be advocating what we in this corner have been advocating through the years. The crown holds the natural resources in trust for all the people.

speechtext: That is national
I do not want to go into the constitutional question in detail today.
You are founding your argument on it.

No. I am not
founding my argument on the constitution as it is today but on something a great deal bigger.
Why don't you establish your basis and proceed.

I am dealing with principles. There may be the complicated legal question of the crown in right of the provinces as against that of the crown in right of the dominion. I do not want to be drawn into that discussion today; I am dealing with the general principle and we believe that what is true of the Dominion government ought to be true of the provinces as well. We are laying down a great general principle which will have to be worked out. If war broke out these constitutional questions would not stand in the way for a minute; the Dominion government would invoke certain residual powers it holds and would manage to make the constitution work. That is the point. An hon. member behind me suggests that the crown is the people. Of course it is. There is a great deal bigger question at issue than that of the respective rights of the provinces and of the dominion. Let me quote still further from the radio speech of the Prime Minister:
I cannot think that any government would be warranted in leaving the air to private 53719-107J
exploitation and not reserving it for development for the use of the people.
It was only a few days after that utterance that the question of radium came up. I think radium deposits are considered to be under the control of the dominion, but when this matter was being considered the government made no effort to apply its own principle. If the principle enunciated by the Prime Minister applies to one particular natural resource it ought to have been applied to radium as well. I think this gives a practical answer to the hon. member for South Toronto (Mr. Geary)-the government took no action even where it had the authority.
Whether or not we like it, to-day the state is intervening more and more in business affairs. I submit that the Duff report and the suggested plans founded thereon go further than most legislation when they attempt to consolidate the railroads in some way or to arrange for their centralized control. We are being forced to advance along socialistic lines. I know there are those who say we should have less government in business, but-
Hear, hear.

The hon. member
for Weyburn (Mr. Young) says, "hear, hear." He has been long enough in Ottawa to know that there is a steady stream of people coming here to secure special favours and that no corporation could exist had it not come to the government for its charter and for special favours.
No.

Industry undoubtedly is in a serious plight to-day. It seems to me that instead of our being lorced tu take over industry', a great many industries will be coming to us. as did the old Canadian Northern, and asking to be taken over. Industry is in a bad way. I do not believe that the industrialist can pay his dividends to-day and at the same time pay decent wages, but when that alternative must be decided I say unhesitatingly that the employees ought to be secured a decent living and their claims should have priority over dividends. If industry as constituted under present conditions cannot grant a decent living to its employees, so much the worse for industry, and in such cases it should be taken over.
Similarly the governments of this country are in a bad way because they are not able to balance their budgets; I do not believe they can, on the one hand, give adequate services to the people and, at the same time,

pay the interest upon their bonded indebtedness. We shall have to say whether the interest upon bonded indebtedness shall have precedence over the sendees needed by the people.

Would
the hon. gentleman allow me to ask a question?

Speaker intervenes upon other occasions.

I recognize that a
great many object to the program which we have in view in that it may undercut what is called the principle of private property. That may be quite true, but I suggest that that principle of private property has been unwarrantedly extended. We create an artificial body which we call a corporation, and then, without imposing upon it any responsibilities, we give it all the privileges of a private person; without its having any soul, we endow it with immortality. I do not think we can allow an assumption of that kind to continue. It may very well be that my home is private property, that other things which 1 use and enjoy are private property, but the original idea of private property should never have been extended to the machinery by which modern production is carried on. It does not belong there at all and ought never to have been extended to such a degree- that will have to be altered. Who can contend for a moment that the Bank of Montreal or the Canadian Pacific Railway are private property in any real sense? pen-a kind very easily made and, unfortunately, easily unmade. There is another kind of money made of high grade paper and with a printing press, and that is the better kind.

Money is nothing of the kind. In the true sense of the word it is a medium of exchange, a system of tickets whereby we exchange goods and services one for another. Speaking in the material sense money is the most important thing in our lives, and it is imperative that we should have a proper amount of it. It is important not to have too much and equally important not to have too little. Why do they want money? Because they must have it if they are to get their livelihood. That is the reason that money is so important to us. The whole standard of living of our people depends upon the amount of money they control, and for the last three years the standard of living has been steadily declining.
It seems to me that the success of any monetary system should be judged by the standard of living which the people can enjoy under it. If our standard of living has been steadily declining, as it has been for three years, then there is something seriously wrong with our money system and we have a prima facie case established against the present system. I have not time today to attempt to deal with the many contributing causes of the crisis. One cause, of course, is the displacement of men by machinery; I will not attempt to deal with that. Another cause is the unequal division of wealth or income, with which I shall have to deal incidentally. The next cause is our antiquated money system, a debt-creating system which has been in use in the so-called civilized world for the last hundred years, under which, according to an
estimate of the League of Nations, there has been built up throughout the world an aggregate debt of over four hundred billions of dollars. I suppose these debts are theoretically or technically payable in gold; yet all the gold in the world amounts to only eleven billion dollars. May I ask how anyone expects to pay in gold even the interest, let alone the principal of this debt of four hundred billion dollars. The interest is not paid in gold but in goods. When it comes to paying international debts they are paid with goods, and (he tariffs which we hear so much about today only serve to impede that payment in goods. Many international debts are today impossible of settlement owing to tariffs and the low world price of export commodities. I believe that any student of the present crisis will agree that the immediate cause of this world situation is the collapse of commodity price levels which started in 1929, and which collapse was brought about by a deflation of the world's credit.
May I quote briefly from Sir William Beveridge, director of the London School of Economics:
This is essentially a money crisis. There is a breakdown in the machinery of exchange. What we have in this crisis is a fall of prices, representing deflation of money.

It is the object of the motion to remove the competitive basis of industry as it now exists, and to supplant it with cooperative effort in which all our citizens will be asked to give of their best in building up a strong and vigorous nation Our design is to eliminate all that

is undesirable in the present economic system, and to keep that which is best, and to build upon that basis. Naturally this implies fundamental changes and a new mental attitude towards our economic problems. It means a considerable extension of the policy of government ownership, government control and regulation, beyond what we now have. I know that some hon. members are horrified at the thought of more government ownership or control, but I should like for a moment to enumerate some of the forms of government control that we now have and with which we come in contact in our daily life.
Takmg the federal government first, it owns or controls the post office. It owns or nominally owns a railway. Then it controls, through the agency of a railway board, railway rates. It owns harbours and canals, and only very recently there oame under the ownership and control of the federal government the radio broadcasting services in Canada. But there is a form of government control and regulation elsewhere b}' the federal government to a far greater extent than exists in any of the directions I have already mentioned. It has been stated in this house and on the public platform by members of the government that but for the tariff now existing in this country many of our industries could not possibly exist. So we see that in the tariff structure of Canada we have another form of government control and regulation. It has also been said by the Prime Minister and others that if the tariff had not been increased to the height it has now reached in Canada, some of these industries would have been driven out of business. So in the tariff we have a form of government control and regulation, and I regard it as a form of government control that acts simply for the protection of capital and in no way for the protection of those who are employed in industry.
In the provincial sphere, we find local governments owning or controlling hydro light and power, telephones, and, what may be of even greater importance to some people, the liquor business. Our provincial governments also have control of the educational facilities of the nation. A great many years ago the education of the rising generation was practically in the hands of private enterprise, but gradually we have reached the stage where private enterprise had to be supplanted by the state, and today education has become almost a state function in all parts of the country.
In the municipal sphere, we find a similar state of affairs. In many of our municipalities 53719-108J
the transportation facilities are owned and controlled by the municipalities. It would be almost unthinkable if the water supply, for instance, of any city were in the hands of private enterprise, or anything else which has to do with the health of the community. Municipalities also control parks and recreation facilities, hospitals, and in some cases cemeteries, as well as looking after the general health of the community. My hon. friend from Southeast Grey (Miss Macpbail) also adds golf courses, but I class them under the head of recreation, and not work.
In addition to what I have already enumerated, we find that various governments have introduced workmen's compensation acts providing for compensation to the man who is injured while at work. Minimum wage laws which affect different industries have also been introduced in different legislatures, and the hours of labour have been controlled. There have been similar enactments put on the statute books in all parts of this dominion, giving a certain control and regulation to the state of the industries affected.
What we are really asking for in this motion is that this idea of state control, ownership and regulation, should be extended a great deal further than obtains at the present time. I know that some hon. members of this house have a horror of the idea of government control or government regulation, but what is the position at the present time? Who is in control of industry in this country? Is it the individual or is it the banks? I venture to assert that most of the industries of this country are at this very moment owned by the banks or the great financial institutions of this country. So therefore when we advocate either state control or government ownership it really resolves itself into the question whether there shall be control and ownership by the banks or control and ownership by the state. And if we put that question plainly to the people of this country I 'have no hesitation in saying that they would prefer state control to banking control. Those who have been in control of the affairs of the nation in recent years have failed to grasp the significance of the vast changes which have been taking place in our midst. For many decades we have been building up a political democracy which finds expression through its representatives in this house. While that is desirable and is something which must be maintained, there has also grown up in this country a power which is a more potent force than parliament itself. I refer to the power of finance. I
1708	COMMONS
Cooperative Commonwealth-Mr. Heaps
am not entirely blaming the financiers for this state of affairs. I blame parliament far more because it ought to be sovereign in the country, and if parliament has allowed the financial interests to have such a controlling influence, then it ought to be the duty of parliament to see that the control of finance and credit should be in its own hands and should be utilized for the benefit of the people as a whole and not for the benefit of financial institutions.
We are told that if we allowed the state to own or control the industries of the country it would be doing away with that private initiative which helps to build up a nation. For a moment or two I want to deal with this question of private initiative, sometimes termed incentive, about which, if this debate :is prolonged, we shall hear a great deal in this house.
I wonder what incentive the average working man has at the present time. Take a man working on the railway. He gives the best years of his life in the service of the railway, helping to build up the system in this country, and after he has worked for ten or fifteen or twenty or twenty-five years what does he find? What is his position at this moment after twenty or twenty-five years of service? He is told that his services are no longer required, and after an experience of unemployment he has to go into the bread line and take his chance with the rest, becoming a recipient of public relief. Is that any incentive, or where is the opportunity of initiative? And yet that is what we find among hundreds of thousands of our people. The average working man who has laboured in industry for ten or twenty or thirty years finds, when he gets old, that he is supplanted by someone who is younger and more vigorous and is therefore able to turn out a larger amount of work because he is more physically fit for the task. We find, therefore that men are thrown into the scrap heap and told to go and shift for themselves, and if they are fortunate enough to reach the age of seventy they will then be entitled to five dollars a week.
Most working men today like farmers live on the borderline of poverty, and these people who have a hard grind to make a living, year in and year out, eking out a mere pittance, hardly able to put anything away for a rainy day, have not much urge in the way of initiative or incentive. I maintain that the very system under which we are living crushes out of the individual that incentive which so many of us would like to see among the people as a whole.

I wonder how many people have been in Ford's factory or any similar institution and had an opportunity of seeing just how much incentive there is for the workers there. The individual merely becomes a cog in the machine. This is true of every industry. Industry has become so specialized in every line of endeavour that at the present time the eight hour day is nothing but a monotonous grind, and instead of the machine becoming the slave of the individual the individual is made the slave of the machine. I entirely disagree with those who suggest that under a sane and more orderly social system there would be no room for that incentive that makes for invention and progress. Let me say something that I have said in this house before, because it is worth repeating. There is one profession whose members do not always regard the dollar as the sole motive for scientific advancement. In most of the engineering lines and among other professions the main motive no doubt is the desire to accumulate a little more wealth. But here may I say a word with respect to the medical profession. In the sphere of medicine it has been a time-honoured custom that those men engaged in research in medical laboratories, those who are able to discover something of advantage to humanity at large, never attempt to use their discoveries as means to gain any commercial benefit for themselves. Such discoveries are given to the world at large so that humanity may be the gainer as a result of the efforts of these research workers.
Even though money has not been the incentive to the medical profession in bringing about these changes which in some way relieve human suffering, I believe I can state with considerable confidence that medicine has kept pace with almost any other branch of scientific activity we know of, so that it ought to be obvious, that given something worth while to strive for, the human being will usually respond, refusing to regard money as the motive for engaging in work of real value. Most people would be satisfied with the thought that anything which they might do to improve conditions in the world at large and to make for a happier life and a better standard of living would bring its own reward.
During the hundred and fifty years or so that capitalism as we know it today has been in operation it has been of some advantage to mankind; it has done certain things which the present generation appreciate. But we say that it has more or less outlived its usefulness; it has reached the stage where it is beginning to decay and is unable to function as a sane

Cooperative Commonwealth-Mr. Heaps
or orderly system. It has almost perfected the art of production. We have produced wealth in abundance, wealth undreamed of a few generations ago; yet capital itself is at this moment rapidly disappearing from our midst. May I here make a distinction between capital and wealth? If the capital of a nation disappears it does not for a moment follow that one iota of wealth will disappear -I am of course referring to finance capital. Although, as pointed out this afternoon by the hon. member for Southeast Grey, a great deal of capital has disappeared from our midst during recent years, the wealth of the country remains intact, and all that is required is a sane system of planning whereby the wheels of industry will be kept running and men engaged in useful production.
Our indictment against capitalism is that it has made man the slave of the machine. On most occasions it has fought every effort made in the past to improve the conditions of the masses. In its competitive character it creates hatreds and jealousies; in its quest for markets it engenders war. It allows wealth to accumulate in superabundance in a few hands while vast numbers live on the border line of poverty and others in actual poverty and want. We in this corner of the house and many others in the house wish to replace these conditions by an economic structure which will really recognize the human being as all-important. Human wellbeing must therefore be the first consideration. We want competition replaced by cooperation. We want the human being to realize that his own and the community's interests are identical and that the wellbeing of the one is the wellbeing of the other. We want to abolish the real causes that lead to war. We want to abolish the idea that the interchange of commodities is a form of warfare, making people realize that, on the contrary, such interchange is the cement that binds nation and nation together. We want to eliminate that competitive individualism with the enormous waste and poverty resulting therefrom. We want to displace all this with an idea which will build up a strong and vigorous nation, where mutual help shall be the dominant factor instead of antagonism. If a labour government were in power today I would expect the faithful service of all citizens. As a writer in a British labour paper stated recently, under a labour government the state would enter upon the task of national reconstruction, keeping always before its eyes the principles of humanity. They should have precedence to profits.
A labour government?

The hon. member for Southeast Grey asks, "a labour government?" I believe that if a labour and farmer government took control of this country we would expect just that thing. As far as I am concerned I do not care whether a government under another label brings in these reforms and fundamental changes in our economic life. What I am anxious to see is that these changes are made. However, I have little hope that any other group or party will be responsible for these changes except that group which happens to sit in this comer of the house. A labour or a farmer government, a combination of both, or the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation if given a mandate by the people, would inaugurate a policy which would govern the nation as though it were an association of citizens, cooperating to provide by the most economical methods for the material needs of all the people, requiring faithful service of all members of this association, and assuring to them a means of living a healthful and decent life.
This afternoon certain statements were made as to the constitutional aspects of this question. Whenever we desire to bring about a fundamental change, particularly in the economic life of the people of this country, we are always told that there is a constitutional difficulty. Let me say that where there is a will to bring about these changes which will improve the lot of millions of our people, then there will be found a way out of these constitutional difficulties. It is only when there is no will that there is no remedy. A few years ago the same constitutional difficulty was raised with regard to old age pensions, but we find that the constitutional objections were overcome and today approximately
45.000	people are receiving the benefits of old age pensions. If it had been necessary for the provinces to agree to certain constitutional changes to make that possible, these
45.000	people probably would not be in receipt of pensions. When the people of this country are prepared to bring about the changed economic conditions which are in keeping with the general terms of the resolutions proposed by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, I think ways and means will be found of adjusting our constitution to meet the needs of the people. As has so often been said by others, the constitution was made for the people of Canada, not the people of Canada for the constitution.

Mr. Speaker, in connection with this resolution I find myself in almost complete agreement with the utterances of those who have preceded me.
1710	COMMONS
Cooperative Commonwealth-Mr. Garland
I regret that no member of any other party in this house has so far taken part in the discussion. I trust that before the debate is concluded we shall have the result of their deliberate consideration with regard to a proposal which is not only fundamental but which is receiving with extraordinaiy rapidity the marked approbation of the people of Canada from coast to coast. Nothing has interested me so much in the last few months as the astonishing display of enthusiasm at meetings wherever this question has been discussed, the proposal to bring into being by constitutional and legal means a new social order has been considered. I wish hon, members could have attended some of these meetings and have heard the expressions of opinion of those who attended, the applause, the condemnation of existing injustices, and the complete agreement in the general denunciation of the inhuman and unsocial character of the economie'order under which at present we are condemned to function.
As I say, I find myself in accord with the words used by the hon. members who have preceded me. They have done something which neither of the old political parties, with all their experience, with all their love for the existing capitalistic system and their reverence for those institutions which they are determined to keep alive, has yet done. We have developed a constructive social plan. It is true that it is tentative in character and will be subject to necessary modifications from time to time, but hon. members on both sides of the house, particularly of the government, have so far utterly failed to offer the people of this country any constructive plan whatever. They have shown that they are bereft of courage and vision in the handling of the situation, even if they have the economic knowledge, which I very seriously doubt.
We have been in an economic tailspin, if I may use the phrase, for three years. We are now entering the fourth year, and any tail-spin which is permitted to go on unchecked will sooner or later bring about the crash. That is just about the stage this country has reached. Even the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) has expressed the gravest alarm at the dangerous financial, commercial and economic condition of our people. But what is he doing about it? What is his plan? Does he think he can make the present social and economic order function intelligently? Does he think that under capitalism he can ever undertake the distribution of the collectively produced wealth of Canada upon a fair and equitable basis? Does he imagine that under

capitalism he will be able to cure unemployment? Does he believe that under capitalism he is going to establish equality of social and economic life for the people of Canada? If he does, then I tell him that he does not know anything about economics.
During the three years of this tailspin we have had no constructive leadership; it has been just a jumping from one crazy idea to another. First, high tariffs; then, rigid deflation ; at another time the expansion of money in order to relieve unemployment; at still another time the contraction of money; and today we have the all-pervading policy of economy. This is the most destructive deflationary policy which could possibly be conceived, and the most stupid which could be inaugurated in a country where, as other speakers have suggested, the only problem is to discover how best to consume the wealth of goods which we are so capable of producing collectively. There has been no intelligent leadership, on the part of either the bankers, the statesmen, the big businessmen or the political parties during the past three years. They have all concentrated with everlasting energy and persistent resolution upon the effort to "just get by" in the hope that some expected upturn which they have no justification to expect, will occur. There has been no application of rationality to the problem; there has been no wish to experiment; there has been no boldness in policy; there has been no understanding of the modern economic world in which we live, in short there has been no leadership.
Debatable as it may be, inadequate as I grant you it possibly is, we in this corner of the house at least are offering to the people some leadership, some way out. You may call it wrong, stupid, and futile. I believe it to be sound, intelligent and rational. If it is not, then in the most friendly sense I challenge hon. members on both sides to disabuse me of my consciousness in this regard. But let me point out for their interest that men who hold infinitely higher positions than I ever hope to attain have already expressed themselves in no uncertain terms on this matter. Let me take words I used last year and use again, the words of Lord Marley, speaking on June 22, 1932 (not long ago), in the House of Lords in Great Britain, that chamber which with the exception of our own upper house is perhaps the greatest bulwark of the existing capitalistic system one can find anywhere on earth. This noble Lord said:
The capitalist system is tottering. Unfortunately we cannot be entirely detached because

Questions
we are affected in the common smash. The difficulty of the system is how to consume the goods which the system is able to produce.
Even he understood that.
The greatest danger in the world from the system-
And I ask hon. members to note these words of his.
-is the danger that the only means of consuming these goods to an adequate extent is by another world war.
Let those significant words sink into the consciousness of hon. members both opposite and around me. One can philosophize at times, but after all we are facing practical difficulties and issues now. I ask hon. members what they conceive to be the cancer, the canker, that is wrecking this civilization as surely as I am standing here. With all the earnestness, sincerity and moderation at my command I say this. That cancer is that we have an	economic	code which	basesits conception of success upon the attainment of wealth. We do not ask how the wealth is attained. It may be by any kind of trickery or chicanery, by stock juggling, by syndicates	formed to	exploit	the	shareholders of a	company;	it may	be	by adozen devices well known	to hon.	gentlemen,
well known to competitive commercialism. But I say to them that the philosophy that underlies and governs such a system belongs to a day of primitive and primeval barbarism and not to a modern Christian civilization. Somebody said this afternoon that there had grown with the system the strange idea that the survival of the fittest was the law which should govern-the law of the jungle.

Before the house rises, I wish
to move a resolution that I promised the last day before the fall adjournment. I move:
That the following resolution passed by the house on October 7, 1932, be rescinded:
"That on and after Monday, the 10th instant, and every day thereafter, government orders shall have precedence over all business except questions by members and notices of motions for production of papers."
And that standing order 15 be adhered to in the same manner as though the session had opened on January 30, 1933.
It will perhaps be recalled that I indicated to the house we would treat private members' days as though the sassion opened on the 30th day of January, and this is to give effect to that understanding. It is well that the motion should be passed now, because tomorrow is
a private members' day, and the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) will be able to continue his remarks.

Motion agreed to.
At six o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
